title: Locard's Exchange Principle: "Every Contact Leaves a Trace" (early 1900s)
explainer: In the early 1900s the French criminologist Edmond Locard, who ran one of the first police crime laboratories in Lyon, formulated forensic science's founding assumption: every contact between two things leaves some trace of that contact. Digital forensics runs on the same logic — a login, a file copy, or a network connection is a 'contact' that leaves traces in logs, timestamps, and metadata, which is why investigators assume evidence survives even when someone tries to cover their tracks. Locard's principle is why forensic examiners go looking for residue instead of assuming a clean system.

title: Clifford Stoll's 75-Cent Discrepancy and the Birth of Digital Forensics (1986)
explainer: In 1986 astronomer-turned-sysadmin Clifford Stoll noticed a 75-cent accounting error on a Lawrence Berkeley Lab computer, traced it to an unauthorized account, and spent the next ten months methodically logging an intruder's every keystroke to track him to a hacker in Hanover, West Germany who was selling stolen data to the KGB. His investigation, recounted in the book The Cuckoo's Egg, is widely regarded as one of the earliest documented examples of digital forensics — treating a computer intrusion as a case to be built from logs and evidence rather than just an outage to patch. It illustrates the patient, evidence-first mindset that modern forensic investigation still depends on.
